idiom_name: custom container class with bind / __rshift__ / match
implementation_notes: Python has no Monad type class and no higher-kinded types, so the pattern is realised by writing a small container (Some/Nothing or Success/Failure) with a unit constructor and a bind method, optionally wired to the >> operator and unwrapped with structural pattern matching. Exceptions already cover much of the Either effect and async/await covers the IO instance, so a hand-written container pays off mainly where failures must be values (validation, pipelines) rather than control flow.
pitfalls: None is both 'no value' and a legitimate value, so absence needs an explicit sentinel or a distinct Nothing class, otherwise bind silently swallows real data.
Exceptions raised inside a step bypass the container entirely unless every step (or bind) wraps its body - that leaves two parallel error channels.
Dynamic typing does not enforce a -> M b: a step that accidentally returns a bare value fails later, far from the mistake.

variants.name: returns containers (Maybe/Result/IOResult)
variants.idiom_name: returns Maybe/Result/IOResult with bind and do-notation
variants.implementation_notes: The returns library supplies typed containers (Maybe, Result, IO, IOResult, Future) with bind/bind_optional/map, a mypy plugin that type-checks the bind signature inside Python's type system, and do-notation for pipelines. Use it when the project is mypy-strict and failures must be values; it is a dependency, not stdlib, so the flat default stays the hand-written container when adding a package is not justified.
pitfalls: returns containers do not capture exceptions: a step that raises aborts the pipeline instead of producing Failure, so boundary calls need explicit wrapping.
The mypy plugin must be configured or the type-safety claim is empty and bind stays as unchecked as a hand-rolled class.

variants.name: async def + await (asyncio coroutines)
variants.implementation_notes: For the IO effect Python's native monadic structure is the coroutine: an async def function is unit, await is bind, and asyncio.gather is the applicative combination of independent effects, with the event loop as the interpreter (scheduling, cancellation, timeouts). Prefer it whenever the effect is I/O; keep explicit containers for failures that must be values rather than exceptions.
variants.code_sketch:
async def report(user_id: str) -> Report:
    user = await users.find(user_id)   # bind: resumes with the value
    orders = await orders.of(user)     # depends on user
    return summarize(user, orders)
pitfalls: A coroutine object that is never awaited does nothing and only emits RuntimeWarning when garbage-collected; the effect runs only when awaited or scheduled.
Blocking calls inside a coroutine stall the whole event loop; they belong in a thread or process executor via run_in_executor/asyncio.to_thread.
Awaiting coroutines sequentially serialises independent operations; use asyncio.gather or TaskGroup when there is no dependency.
